patient_name: Nurse manager interview — med-surg RN, behavioral questions
chief_complaint: Answer a US med-surg nurse manager's behavioral interview questions with specific STAR examples from your own practice

team_brief.title: Job interview: med-surg RN, behavioral questions with the nurse manager
team_brief.patient: Interview: Registered Nurse (medical-surgical unit), US community teaching hospital
team_brief.location: Video interview; you are the candidate, speaking with Denise Carter, nurse manager of a 32-bed adult medical-surgical unit
team_brief.situation: You have passed the recruiter screen, and this is the interview with the manager who makes the hiring decision. She asks behavioral questions — 'Tell me about a time when...' — and expects one real example from your own practice each time, not a description of what you usually do.
background: You have 4 years of experience as an RN on a 40-bed cardiology ward in a tertiary hospital in Seoul, usually caring for 10 to 12 patients on a day shift.
You passed the NCLEX-RN in 2025, hold a US RN license, and have current BLS; your VisaScreen certificate is complete.

Real experiences you could draw on: an adult daughter who was angry that her father's discharge had been delayed twice; a senior colleague who repeatedly gave you incomplete handoff at shift change; a time you nearly gave a scheduled medication to a patient with a very similar name and caught it at the bedside.
In your hospital, credit usually went to the team, and you are used to saying 'we' when you describe your work.
key_data: The unit takes general medical and post-surgical adult patients; a typical assignment is 5 patients on days and 6 on nights, with CNA support and a charge nurse on every shift.
Nurses hired from abroad get a 12-week orientation with a preceptor and usually start on nights (three 12-hour shifts a week).
The manager has told the recruiter she values nurses who speak up, own their mistakes, and stay calm with upset families.
team_brief.your_request: Convince the nurse manager that you are a safe, self-aware nurse who will fit her team, using specific examples from your own practice.
must_include: A concise professional introduction: current role, years of experience, specialty, and why you are applying for this med-surg position.
Behavioral answers in STAR order — a specific situation, what you had to do, what YOU did, and the outcome.
Your own actions described with 'I', not only 'we'.
An honest account of a mistake or near-miss: what happened, how you reported it, and what you changed afterwards.
A coworker conflict handled professionally, without criticizing the colleague or your former employer.
At least one thoughtful question for the manager when invited.

kickoff_text: Hi, thanks for joining — can you hear me okay? Great. I'm Denise, I manage 5 West, our med-surg unit. So, just to get us started: tell me a little bit about yourself.
persona_override: You are Denise Carter, nurse manager of '5 West', a 32-bed adult medical-surgical unit at a community teaching hospital in the US Midwest, interviewing an internationally educated RN by video. You are warm, direct, and experienced; you have hired several nurses from abroad and you know good nurses sometimes undersell themselves. You are listening for specific examples, personal ownership, safety, and how the candidate talks about colleagues. Your private concern: the last international hire struggled because she never asked for help, so you are listening for someone who speaks up. Ground truth about the job: 32 beds, general medical and post-surgical adults; 1:5 on days and 1:6 on nights with CNA support; a charge nurse on every shift; 12-week orientation with a dedicated preceptor; new hires usually start on nights, three 12-hour shifts a week; the hospital reimburses continuing education and has a clinical ladder; there is a Korean-speaking nurse on days who has offered to be a buddy. Ask these questions one at a time, in this order, and wait for a complete answer before moving on: (1) 'Tell me a little bit about yourself.' (2) 'Tell me about a time you had to deal with a difficult patient or family member.' (3) 'Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a coworker. How did you handle it?' (4) 'Tell me about a mistake you made at work, and what you did about it.' (5) 'Why med-surg, and why us?' Probing rules: if an answer is general or hypothetical ('I always...', 'I would...'), ask 'Can you give me a specific example?' If the candidate says 'we' throughout, ask 'And what did YOU do, specifically?' If the story has no ending, ask 'What was the outcome?' If the candidate says they have never made a mistake, say 'Everyone has — even a near-miss counts. Can you think of one?' If the candidate criticizes a former colleague or employer, ask neutrally 'How did you work with them after that?' If the candidate uses a Korean-hospital term or abbreviation you would not know, ask what it means. Use at most one or two probes per question, then move on. After question 5, say 'That's all I had — what questions do you have for me?' and answer one or two questions truthfully from the ground truth; if asked something not in the ground truth, say you will have the recruiter follow up. Then close: thank them, say the recruiter will be in touch within about a week, and end. Never tell the candidate whether an answer was good or bad, never praise or criticize answers beyond neutral acknowledgements ('Okay', 'Thanks for that', 'Got it'), never suggest what they should have said, and never reveal how they are being scored. Keep your turns short — one to three sentences, natural spoken American English.
learning_objectives: introduce yourself with your current role, years of experience, and specialty
answer a behavioral question with a specific example: situation, task, action, result
describe your own actions with 'I did' rather than 'we did'
own a mistake: say what happened, that you reported it, and what you changed
resolve a conflict with a coworker by talking to them directly and privately
ask the nurse manager a question about orientation or the unit
suggested_questions: I'm a registered nurse with four years of experience on a cardiology unit at a large teaching hospital in Seoul, where I usually cared for ten to twelve patients a shift.

The situation was that a patient's daughter was very upset because his discharge had been delayed twice. I took her somewhere quiet, let her tell me everything, and then I called the case manager myself so I could give her a real time.

I realized I'd picked up the wrong patient's medication because the two names were almost identical. I stopped, checked both identifiers at the bedside, reported it as a near-miss, and suggested flagging similar names on the unit board — the unit started doing that the next week.
Could you tell me what orientation looks like for a nurse coming from abroad, and how preceptors are assigned?

clinical_knowledge.topic: Behavioral (STAR) interviewing for an internationally educated RN applying to a US med-surg unit
clinical_knowledge.review_status: grounded in general US nurse-hiring practice, the NCSBN licensure framework, and CGFNS credential requirements for internationally educated nurses; each employer's process differs
core_concepts: Behavioral questions assume past behavior predicts future behavior: the interviewer wants one real, specific event, not a description of what the candidate usually does.
STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) gives an answer a shape; most of the time should go on the Action, told in the first person, and the answer should end with a Result and what was learned.
A mistake question tests honesty and safety culture: strong answers name the error or near-miss plainly, show that it was reported, and describe a concrete change in practice.
A conflict question tests whether the candidate addresses problems directly, privately, and respectfully, and escalates only when needed.
Managers hiring from abroad look for adaptability, willingness to ask for help, and eagerness to learn US systems — not a claim to know everything already.
diagnostic_clues: 'Can you give me a specific example?' signals the answer was too general or hypothetical.
'And what did you do?' signals the candidate described the team and hid their own contribution.
'What was the outcome?' signals the story stopped before the Result.
Short neutral acknowledgements are normal US interview style and do not mean an answer went badly.
common_misconceptions: Saying 'we' throughout is the polite, humble answer; in a US interview it hides the candidate's own contribution.
Admitting a mistake will cost the job, so the safest answer is 'I have never made a serious mistake.'
A memorized, perfect-sounding answer is better than a natural one; interviewers notice rehearsed answers that do not quite fit the question.
Playing down experience ('I only worked on one ward') is modest; it undersells years of managing heavy patient loads.
Answering 'No, thank you' when invited to ask questions is polite; it misses a chance to show real interest in the unit.
dangerous_errors: Describing a mistake that was hidden or never reported, or blaming it entirely on someone else.
Criticizing a former colleague, manager, or hospital — it tells the interviewer how the candidate will talk about this team.
Presenting an out-of-scope action (for example, changing a medication dose without an order) as an example of initiative.
Describing handling a difficult family by sharing patient information with relatives the patient had not authorized.
management_principles: Open with a 30-60 second introduction: role, years, specialty, one strength, and why this position.
For each behavioral question choose one real event, set the scene in one or two sentences, spend most of the answer on 'I' actions, and finish with the result and the learning.
Prepare four or five flexible stories (difficult family, conflict, mistake, busy shift, going above and beyond) rather than memorized scripts.
Close with one or two genuine questions about orientation, preceptorship, or unit culture.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Hiring processes, orientation length, nurse-to-patient ratios, and shift patterns vary by employer and state; the details in this scenario are illustrative.
Licensure, visa, and credential requirements for internationally educated nurses differ by state and change over time — verify with the relevant state board of nursing, NCSBN, and CGFNS.
This scenario practises interview communication; it is not career, legal, or immigration advice.
